topic: JO/COS absorption, plantilla vacancies, and professionalization funding
summary: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. led the inquiry into 919,868 JO and COS workers, vacant plantilla positions, and the absence of measurable absorption and vacancy-reduction targets. CSC described preferential rating, qualification requirements, Prime ESG, agency optimization, and a target covering 40 agencies, but said it could not establish a direct correlation between the programs and JO/COS absorption. The agency distinguished regular and necessary functions that should be staffed permanently from temporary or episodic work, and proposed reviews of LGU personnel-service caps and DBM's scrap-and-build policy. Representative Elijah San Fernando and Representative Kaloy Bulilla raised worker precarity, political accommodation, public-sector unionism, and a DSWD worker's case, while CSC discussed joint work with DBM and COA and possible benefits coverage. Representative Democrito Mendoza questioned 224999 vacancies, examination pass rates, and proposed equivalency legislation; CSC said the principal problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete vacancies, staffing constraints, and merit-and-fitness concerns. The issue remained unresolved, with several administrative and legislative follow-ups contemplated.
question: The committee sought to establish how CSC would reduce plantilla vacancies and government-wide reliance on job-order (JO) and contract-of-service (COS) workers, including whether qualified long-serving workers could be absorbed into permanent positions. Members also asked what measurable results would come from the proposed professionalization and modernization allocations and whether CSC would support legislative and monitoring mechanisms.
agency_position: CSC said it could facilitate eligibility, improve HR systems, monitor or analyze JO/COS deployment, and recommend legislative and administrative changes, but could not guarantee absorption into permanent civil service positions. It distinguished workers performing regular and necessary functions, who should be reduced or regularized through proper staffing, from workers performing temporary or episodic functions, for whom JO/COS arrangements remained necessary.
outcome: The committee obtained CSC's explanation of the existing preferential-rating, modernization, optimization, and public-sector unionism measures, but no government-wide numerical targets for vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption were committed. Legislative equivalency, monitoring, LGU staffing limits, and the precise scope of CSC jurisdiction remained open for further policy or legislative action.

positions.position: Pressed CSC to provide government-wide, measurable targets for filling vacancies, reducing JO/COS reliance, monitoring workers, and demonstrating results from the professionalization and modernization allocations.

Supported regularization or reduction of JO/COS use for workers performing regular and necessary functions, while recognizing that some temporary work required such arrangements. He identified perpetual hiring and political accommodation as major concerns.
Supported the CSC budget and sought a remedy for the precarious situation of a DSWD JO worker transferred to Pasay LGU.
Sought a legislative equivalency pathway for qualified long-serving workers, questioned persistent vacancies and examination pass rates, and urged CSC support for House Bills 93 and 92.
Recognized the operational importance of JOs and COS workers but said legal and governance constraints had to be addressed while CSC continued reviewing policies.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked what CSC was doing about unfilled plantilla positions and continued reliance on JO and COS workers. He cited CSC's inventory of 919,868 JO and COS workers and asked for a government-wide plan to match qualified workers with vacant positions, help workers obtain eligibility, and provide measurable targets and a timeline.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC was reluctant to give absorption targets because appointing authorities must apply qualification requirements to positions. CSC's current measure was preferential rating for JO and COS workers in the civil service examination, while workers still had to meet education, experience, training, and eligibility requirements.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official described the preferential-rating measure as a 70% grade score and a 10% avenue to enter government service, subject to passing the civil service eligibility examination and meeting other qualification requirements.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said workers with ten years of experience could apply the preferential rating, with five years satisfying the government-service experience requirement. Training and education remained potential barriers, although workers meeting first-level or second-level educational qualifications could enter government service if the other requirements were met.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal asked when the change was implemented. The CSC official answered that it was implemented early this year, after the budget deliberations.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official reported an increase in applicants and passers under the preferential-rating measure but said CSC could not establish a direct correlation between those measures and JO/COS absorption. CSC would continue working to make absorption more efficient and accessible.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal pressed CSC for a concrete response, noting that departments issue plantilla positions while qualified JO and COS workers remain outside the regular service.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC needed a data-management system to establish the relationship between the preferential-rating program and absorption. CSC could not guarantee employment because qualification standards still applied, and the Commission was not generally empowered to employ JOs and COS workers; the official suggested reviewing the laws, with legislation potentially addressing the issue.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited the proposed CSC civil service professionalization and workplace cooperation allocation of 725,700,000 and asked what measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COS workers Congress should expect.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited budget notes showing 202 unfilled CSC proper positions and 28 unfilled positions in the other CSC unit identified in the transcript as 'CSV.'

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC did not have indicators establishing a correlation between the spending and reductions in JO/COS reliance. The official emphasized that JOs and COS workers were not government employees under civil service jurisdiction and were subject to regulations issued by DBM.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal argued that civil service should monitor JOs and COS workers, particularly because many had worked in government for more than ten years, and asked whether the CSC official agreed.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official agreed that, ideally, CSC could design a system to monitor JOs and COS workers, but did not present an existing system or numerical target.

thread.speaker: Representative Roberto Nazal Jr.
thread.said: Nassal cited the proposed Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project funding of 1,450,000,000 and asked what measurable improvements would be delivered by the end of 2027 in hiring time, appointment processing, vacancy filling, HR records, and payroll. He requested numerical targets, metrics, or key result areas to be reported to Congress.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said Prime ESG, replacing Prime HRM, was intended to improve recruitment and selection, performance management, learning and development, and rewards and incentives through the HRM information system. The stated PCSMP target was to reach 40 agencies across all sectors, but no vacancy or JO/COS-absorption target was provided.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official agreed that some long-serving workers performing regular and necessary functions should already have been made permanent. However, COS and JO arrangements remained important for temporary or episodic work, including welfare distribution, and it would be financially irresponsible to make those workers permanent.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official proposed reviewing LGU personnel-service caps with DILG and DBM, considering regulation of JO/COS numbers in LGUs, and improving CSC assistance to LGUs in recruitment and appointments. The official said 70% of the total number of JOs and COS workers in government were in LGUs.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said CSC was discussing the issue and hoped within this year to recommend a way forward on whether mandatory LGU positions should be mandatory or optional, including the effect on LGUs' ability to create plantilla positions for long-serving JO and COS workers.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official recommended that DBM move away from scrap-and-build as the default policy so agencies could create legitimately needed positions without first identifying positions to scrap. The official also supported analyzing obsolete vacant positions and removing them from the plantilla inventory when justified.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official proposed agency-by-agency staffing analysis and possible trigger points for automatic review when an agency repeatedly hired JOs or COS workers for the same position over a number of years. The stated objective was to minimize the first category of workers performing regular, desirable, and necessary functions while retaining JO/COS arrangements for temporary and episodic work.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the DBM-CSC joint memorandum circular required agencies to maintain updated inventories showing where JOs and COS workers were deployed and what functions they performed. Better implementation and analytics could provide the evidence needed for policies facilitating entry into government service, although CSC could not guarantee absorption at that time.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official described political and electoral realities, particularly in local governments, as part of the reason JO and COS arrangements persisted, while maintaining that these workers were essential to service delivery. The official said legal barriers to integration had to be addressed and that CSC would continue reviewing and rationalizing policies.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando agreed that some JOs and COS workers were essential but said perpetual use of such arrangements created the problem. He identified political accommodation, especially in LGUs, as a concern, and the chair indicated agreement.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando asked about the public-sector unionism subprogram, citing an allocation of around 30,000 pesos to 88,000 pesos per regional office and asking about its outputs and targets.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the program covered organizing and registering public-sector employee organizations, encouraging their creation, recognizing exclusive bargaining units, and registering collective negotiation agreements. The official cited a target to recognize organizations within seven days.

thread.speaker: Representative Elijah San Fernando
thread.said: San Fernando raised the precarious situation of JO and COS workers and said the issue required political reform. He deferred additional questioning to a second round.

thread.speaker: Representative Kaloy Bulilla
thread.said: Bulilla manifested support for passage of the CSC budget but raised the case of a DSWD job-order worker transferred from the national central office to the local government of Pasay. He sought CSC assistance on the worker's situation.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC had not clearly had jurisdiction over JOs and COS workers under the earlier framework, but the President asked CSC to participate in formulating the joint memorandum circular with DBM and COA. CSC interpreted the circular as covering JO/COS workers' entitlement to the seven-day solo-parent leave benefit, subject to refining the mechanism and coordination with DBM.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta explained that CSC's participation in the joint memorandum circular gave it jurisdiction to issue rules concerning JOs and COS workers to that extent, including the application of the solo-parent law to such workers in DSWD.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said the civil service examination passing rate was 80% in the context of the preferential-rating discussion, but clarified that five years of JO service did not automatically create a permanent appointment. Workers remained subject to the necessary qualifications and availability of a permanent position item.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked about 224999 vacant plantilla positions as of July and whether the figure came from CSC or DBM. Acosta answered that it came from the inventory of government human resources.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza said the number of vacant positions remained at roughly the same level and asked for the plan to reduce it, including whether some positions were obsolete.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said there was anecdotal evidence that agencies kept obsolete positions vacant for scrap-and-build purposes. He recommended moving away from scrap-and-build as the default, evaluating genuine agency needs, and having the optimization program monitor long-vacant positions.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC had met workers halfway through a preferential-rating policy: ten years of COS or JO service could provide 10 points, provided the worker had served five years in the position.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked whether CSC would support House Bill 93, an equivalency bill under which at least three years of satisfactory service and demonstrated competence could establish eligibility. He offered to work with CSC on a legislative solution.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said CSC did not have a shortage of eligible applicants, reporting that it produced 160 plus thousand eligibles every year compared with 14,000 positions. He identified the main problems as agencies keeping obsolete vacancies, difficulties creating positions, and LGU personnel-service caps, rather than a lack of eligibles.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza questioned the civil service examination pass rate, citing figures in the transcript as 158080%, 75, 80%, and 15% nationwide, with a separate barangay figure of 25% and 48%. He argued that the results were discouraging.

thread.speaker: CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta
thread.said: Acosta said he personally took the examination whenever it was administered and vouched for the fairness of the items. He attributed the low passing rate to the quality of education and the examinees, not to poor examination questions.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza again asked whether CSC would support an equivalency bill allowing workers with fifteen years or ten years of service, or at least three years of good service, to qualify for permanent positions.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official opposed an automatic three-year equivalency because it could encourage LGUs to hire unqualified people and wait three years to qualify them. The official said CSC's bottom line was to preserve merit and fitness, while noting that the view expressed was personal and not necessarily the Commission's formal position.

thread.speaker: Representative Democrito Mendoza
thread.said: Mendoza asked whether CSC was open to House Bill 92, which would create an independent public-sector labor dispute mechanism and alter labor representation in the PSLMC, including in light of ILO Convention 151.

thread.speaker: CSC official
thread.said: The official said labor representatives already participated in the PSLMC and regional congresses, from which labor-sector representatives would be nominated. When the chair asked about supporting the bills, the official said there was no problem with the proposed representation and noted that the committee had previously discussed the matter.

topic: Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and digital transformation
summary: CSC presented the PCSMP as a central part of its digital transformation, covering Prime ESG, HRMIS plus payroll, a national learning platform, electronic administrative justice, and a civil-service data management system. The agency cited a proposed PCSMP allocation of about 1.34 billion in the budget breakdown, while the opening presentation separately cited 453 million for implementation. Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. pressed for measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and JO/COS dependence, but CSC acknowledged that it had no indicators establishing those correlations and could not guarantee absorption into the civil service. A committee member confirmed that the contact center used written referrals and that CSC's electronic case system could track cases nationwide. Representative Ryan questioned cybersecurity, online oath-taking authentication, SALN rules, and the failed data-center bidding; CSC undertook to submit a cybersecurity cost breakdown and defended the failed bidding as a privacy safeguard. Representative Elijah San Fernando raised delayed administrative cases, and CSC said CLASS would be implemented in 2027 to enable online filing and digital transmission of case records.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and related digital-transformation spending would produce measurable improvements in recruitment, appointment processing, HR records, payroll, case resolution, cybersecurity, and service delivery. Members also asked whether CSC had concrete targets for reducing vacancies and dependence on job-order and contract-of-service workers, and whether safeguards would protect sensitive personnel and SALN data.
agency_position: CSC said modernization and digitalization were necessary to improve HR governance, appointment processing, learning, payroll, records, administrative justice, and public assistance. It described planned systems and implementation targets, but acknowledged that it did not yet have measurable indicators linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption and did not provide a specific cybersecurity or CLASS budget breakdown during the hearing.
outcome: The committee received CSC's explanation of the planned modernization systems and implementation timetable, but the agency did not provide the requested measurable targets linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction, hiring time, or JO/COS absorption. Cybersecurity cost disaggregation was requested for later submission, while CLASS and the data-management systems remained implementation commitments rather than completed outcomes.

positions.position: Modernization spending should be tied to measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and reliance on JOs and COs, with numerical targets and reports to Congress.
Digital expansion required a specific cybersecurity budget and strong authentication and privacy safeguards, particularly for online oath-taking, electronic filing, SALN data, and the data center.
Long delays in administrative cases were unacceptable, and CLASS should be funded and implemented to accelerate case transmission and disposition.

topic: Civil-service examinations, eligibility, and equivalency pathways
summary: Representative Nassal pressed the CSC for a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and concrete results from proposed programs addressing vacancies and dependence on about 919,868 JO and COS workers. The CSC described preferential rating, including the 70% grade score, 10% avenue, and experience-based treatment, but said it could not guarantee appointments or establish a direct correlation with absorption. Representative Ismula raised possible preferential eligibility for IPMRs, and the CSC said it could work toward extending coverage after consultations and subject to legal requirements. Representative Mendoza later urged support for House Bill 93, which would create an equivalency pathway after at least three years of satisfactory service, but the CSC warned that this could encourage agencies to retain unqualified hires and undermine merit and fitness. The CSC said it was producing more than 160 thousand eligibles annually and that the central problems were vacancies, obsolete positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates rather than a shortage of eligibles. The hearing ended without a clear CSC commitment to support House Bill 93 or deliver numerical vacancy and absorption targets, although the agency undertook related work on IPMR preferential rating, modernization guidance, and JO/COS regulation.
question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC would help qualified JO and COS workers obtain eligibility, fill vacant plantilla positions, and reduce reliance on contractual arrangements. Members also examined preferential-rating and equivalency pathways, civil-service examination standards and pass rates, and the CSC's position on related legislation.
agency_position: The CSC said preferential rating could help qualified JO, COS, and potentially IPMR workers obtain eligibility, but it did not guarantee appointment because education, training, experience, eligibility, and position-specific qualification standards still applied. The agency maintained that the main problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete or unavailable positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates; it cautioned that automatic equivalency after three years could undermine merit and fitness.
outcome: The CSC explained its existing preferential-rating pathway and indicated that IPMR coverage could be expanded subject to legal and qualification requirements. The broader issues of measurable vacancy-reduction targets, automatic equivalency under House Bill 93, and the causes of low examination pass rates remained open.

positions.position: The CSC should produce measurable government-wide targets and timelines to fill vacancies, monitor JOs and COS workers, reduce contractual dependence, and demonstrate concrete results from modernization spending.
The CSC should consider preferential eligibility treatment for IPMRs and support improved compensation and benefits for government personnel.
The CSC budget should be supported, while the continuing JO and COS problem and the treatment of experienced contractual workers should be addressed.

The CSC should support House Bill 93 to create an equivalency pathway for experienced, competent government workers and should address low examination pass rates and the lack of a pathway to permanent employment.

topic: CSC compliance and enforcement of personnel rules
summary: Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula questioned how the CSC enforced its expanded gambling ban and whether it covered online gambling. The CSC said complaints could be filed anonymously through contact centers and complaints desks in regional and field offices, and Assistant Commissioner Ariel Ronquillo said the prohibition covered both on-site and online gambling. Ismula also asked about preferential civil-service eligibility for IPMRs; the CSC said it would consult Indigenous Peoples communities and could develop a preferential-rating system, potentially crediting one to three years of representative service toward a five-year experience requirement, subject to law. The member raised a 2,000 pesos compensation reform and House Bill Number 3874, and the CSC expressed support for increased benefits and continued discussions with DBM. Rep. Isabel Segabaria then challenged the CSC's authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule. The CSC acknowledged the need for legal basis but defended the rule under the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, leaving the scope of the agency's authority unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish how the CSC monitored and enforced its expanded gambling prohibition, whether it could provide preferential civil-service eligibility treatment for indigenous peoples mandatory representatives (IPMRs), and what reforms it supported for government compensation. It also sought to clarify whether the CSC had statutory authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule.
agency_position: The CSC said gambling was prohibited both on-site and online and that compliance could be monitored through complaints received by its contact center and complaints desks in regional and field offices. It indicated that preferential eligibility treatment for IPMRs could be developed subject to law, while defending the common-law nepotism rule as an anti-circumvention measure grounded in Supreme Court reasoning, although it acknowledged that an administrative rule must have legal basis.
outcome: The gambling-ban questions were answered with the CSC's position that online gambling was already covered and that complaints systems provided the monitoring mechanism. The IPMR eligibility and compensation matters were left at the level of proposed study, consultation, and continuing dialogue, while the statutory authority for including common-law relationships in the nepotism rule remained contested.

thread.speaker: A CSC agency official
thread.said: The official recognized the validity of the concern and agreed that the CSC could not create a rule without legal basis that would prejudice affected persons. The official nevertheless defended the rule as preventing favoritism and relied on Supreme Court pronouncements that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.

thread.said: The official said the same principle had been applied to designations of relatives, even though designation was not expressly covered by the statutory definition of nepotism. The commission's position was that a common-law partner stood in the same place as a spouse for purposes of preventing the same evil.
